sections.title: A tour of the platform museum

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The platform museum occupies the former waiting area and several small buildings. Start at the cross marked in the centre of the site plan. North is shown at the top.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The restored ticket booth is south of the junction, closest to the bottom of the plan. It is small enough that we will visit it in pairs.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The signal cabin stands to the east of the junction. Look for the steps leading up from the right-hand path.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The parcel store is north of the junction, at the top of the site. The red shutters on its doorway are kept closed to protect the display.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The waiting shelter sits west of the junction. It is the open-fronted building along the left-hand path.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Inside the ticket booth, the guide will demonstrate a stamp. The tickets used for this are modern copies.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The cabin is narrow, so six visitors may enter at a time. The rest of the group can watch from the path.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Put wet coats on the rack outside the parcel store. This keeps the floor around the display dry.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The silent film in the shelter lasts eight minutes. The other film is longer and is shown only on special evenings.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: A yellow sign shows the next departure point. The blue signs belong to the old station and are part of the collection.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: There is a notebook for comments on the bench by the exit. Tell us which part of the route you found easiest to follow.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The tour ends back at the junction. Leave the narrow path clear for the people joining the next group.

script.speaker: Isabel
script.text: We need to agree on our classroom demonstration about how fabrics behave after wetting. The goal is a comparison that another group can repeat.

script.speaker: Drew
script.text: All right. Let’s go through the details.

script.speaker: Isabel
script.text: Change in width is our first measurement. We could compare colours later, and thickness would need equipment we do not have.

script.speaker: Drew
script.text: The samples will dry on the bench. A warm cabinet would speed one part of the process, and hanging them might stretch the edges.

script.speaker: Isabel
script.text: We will use a cutting template. Drawing freehand would make comparison harder, and the ruler alone does not hold the outline in place.

script.speaker: Drew
script.text: Isabel will borrow the measuring tools this afternoon. Drew already has the fabric, and Marta is only joining the final discussion.

script.speaker: Isabel
script.text: Drew will prepare the strips. It makes sense to keep all the pieces from the same piece of fabric together.

script.speaker: Drew
script.text: Marta will check the written method. We want someone who did not set up the trial to see whether our instructions make sense.

script.speaker: Isabel
script.text: Use a washable pencil for the marks. The permanent marker changed the appearance of the edge in our rehearsal.

script.speaker: Drew
script.text: Take the first measurement before adding water. Otherwise we will not know the starting width.

script.speaker: Isabel
script.text: Write the drying period in minutes. We can compare it with another group’s record without converting the units.

script.speaker: Drew
script.text: Keep the dry strips in separate envelopes. It will be easier to find the correct strip when we write up the results.

script.speaker: Isabel
script.text: Once the first comparison is complete, we can decide whether a second fabric is worth adding. Keep the original observations even if the result surprises us.

sections.title: What makes a surface easy to grip?

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Today we will compare surfaces used for handles and steps. The important question is how much the object resists sliding in the conditions in which it is used.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The force that opposes sliding is called friction. Its direction depends on the movement that is occurring or about to occur.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Place the block on a tilting board. Raise one end slowly while keeping the other end in the same position.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Increase the angle until the block begins to slide. The first movement is the point you should note.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Keep the mass of the block the same throughout. Changing the block at the same time would make the comparison harder to interpret.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Look for loose dust before repeating the test. Dust can change what actually touches the board.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Use tape to mark where the block starts. The location should be the same each time.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Give each wet surface the same amount of water. Otherwise one test might use a damp patch and the next a puddle.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: A support can keep the board at a known angle while you measure it. Check that it cannot shift under the weight of the block.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The second surface is rubber. We will compare it with the smooth wooden board before trying other materials.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: State the direction in which the surface was tested. A pattern of ridges might resist sliding across it differently from sliding along it.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Use those observations to describe a particular pairing of materials. The same surface may behave differently when the object, direction or conditions change.
